source_refs.note: Topic 11.5.1, printed pages 253-254. The Interesting Information box on haloalkanes is carried as a sentence.

blocks.text: Substitution reactions of alkanes take place in the presence of light energy through the formation of highly reactive free radicals. An example is the replacement of a hydrogen of an alkane by a halogen atom, halogenation: alkanes react with chlorine and bromine in sunlight or UV light with successive replacement of hydrogen atoms by halogens, the extent of halogenation depending on the amount of halogen used. Reaction with fluorine is highly violent and gives a mixture of carbon, fluorinated alkanes and hydrofluoric acid; iodine does not substitute directly because the reaction is too slow and reversible. The order of reactivity is F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

blocks.alt: Top left: homolytic fission of Cl:Cl into two chlorine radicals and heterolytic fission of A:B into A+ and B-. Bottom: the three steps of the chlorination of methane, initiation, propagation and termination, with equations, and the successive products chloromethane to tetrachloromethane.
blocks.caption: Bond breaking and the free radical chlorination of methane (original diagram after Figures 11.5 and 11.6 and topics 11.3 to 11.5.1).
blocks.long_description: A bond can break evenly, each atom keeping one electron to give reactive free radicals, or unevenly, one atom taking both electrons to give ions. Alkanes resist polar reagents because their bonds are non-polar and strong, but ultraviolet light splits chlorine homolytically and the chlorine radical starts a chain: it pulls a hydrogen from methane to leave a methyl radical, which takes a chlorine from another chlorine molecule and releases a new chlorine radical, and so on, until two radicals meet and the chain ends. Repeated substitution gives chloromethane, dichloromethane, chloroform and carbon tetrachloride, and the trace of ethane from two methyl radicals combining is evidence for the mechanism.

items: Initiation: the first step, in which the halogen-halogen bond breaks using energy from UV light: Cl2 with hv gives Cl. + Cl.

Propagation: the second step, in which the radicals formed attack the alkane molecule and generate more free radicals: CH4 + Cl. gives CH3. + HCl, and CH3. + Cl2 gives CH3Cl + Cl. By repetition of this step a mixture of halogen-substituted products (chloroalkanes) is obtained.

Termination: the final step, in which two free radicals react together to form a product. A chlorine radical and an alkyl radical may combine to give a chloroalkane, two chlorine radicals may re-form Cl2, or two alkyl radicals may merge to give an alkane with double the number of carbon atoms; this last mode is rare and gives only traces, but its occurrence is evidence of the free radical mechanism.

blocks.text: The more chlorine in the mixture to start with, the greater the proportion of chlorine atoms in the chloroalkanes formed: chloromethane CH3Cl, dichloromethane CH2Cl2, trichloromethane CHCl3 (chloroform) and tetrachloromethane CCl4 (carbon tetrachloride) by further substitution with chlorine radicals. Haloalkanes are anaesthetic, their anaesthetic power increasing with the number of halogen atoms, and their use as laboratory solvents is strictly monitored because they are toxic.

blocks.prompt: Predict the products of the free radical chlorination of ethane, and state the conditions under which a mixture of halogenoalkanes is obtained (Quick Check 11.3d, e).
blocks.explanation: In UV light with chlorine, ethane gives chloroethane first, then by further substitution dichloroethanes (1,1- and 1,2-), trichloroethanes and so on up to hexachloroethane, plus HCl, and traces of butane from two ethyl radicals combining. A mixture results whenever the reaction is run in light with chlorine present in excess or allowed to continue, since each chloroalkane can be substituted again.

items: Halogenation in UV light by free radicals; reactivity F2 (violent) greater than Cl2 greater than Br2 greater than I2 (no direct substitution).

Initiation (Cl2 to 2 Cl.), propagation (CH4 + Cl. to CH3. + HCl; CH3. + Cl2 to CH3Cl + Cl.), termination (radicals combine; trace ethane proves the mechanism); successive products CH3Cl, CH2Cl2, CHCl3, CCl4.
